picks.why: The Cognac house founded in 1765 by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer who had served the French crown, and a blender that buys eaux-de-vie across the crus. Its V.S descends from the Three Star cognac a great-grandson of the founder classed in 1865, and at 40 per cent it is the young cognac a guest names when he asks for cognac by brand.
picks.note: The label prints Hennessy Very Special with V.S beneath; confirm the form the bottle shows today. Keep the Library's 'largest cognac house' wording out of the why: it is a ranking. Hennessy is part of the Moët Hennessy group; the house, not the group, is the producer.

picks.why: A Cognac house dated to 1724 that blends only from the Grande and Petite Champagne crus. Its cellar master André Renaud made the first VSOP Fine Champagne in 1927, so this one bottle teaches both the VSOP grade and what Fine Champagne means on a label.
picks.note: Sources disagree on the blend (85 and 15 per cent, or at least half Grande Champagne) and on the average age; take both from the house's own sheet or leave them out. One timeline puts 1724 on the VSOP itself, which is a parsing error. The house belongs to Rémy Cointreau.

picks.why: A Cognac house founded in 1715 by Jean Martell from Jersey. Cordon Bleu, created by Édouard Martell in 1912, is built around eaux-de-vie of the Borderies, the smallest cru, and is the bottling that shows what Borderies brings to a blend.
picks.note: The owner's shelf holds Martell XO (martell-xo), a different bottling from Cordon Bleu; the author may prefer to make the shelf bottle the flagship so the page and the shelf meet, and should say which. Sources call Cordon Bleu an XO; Wikipedia says it carries no age designation; confirm the label. The Borderies share (about half) rests on one source.

picks.why: The Cognac house of Jarnac, built on the Charente, whose blender Louis Renard set out its first core range of Napoléon in 1909 and VSOP in 1910. The VSOP is the round, cask led cognac many bars pour for a Sidecar or a Vieux Carré.
picks.note: The founding date is disputed: 1828 on the house's own heritage page and Beam Suntory's timeline, 1835 elsewhere; use the house's date or none. The Napoléon link is legend and must be told as legend if at all. Ownership has moved (Beam Suntory, then Campari); confirm before naming a parent.

picks.why: A Grande Champagne house whose 1840 Original Formula, first released in 2011, recreates a three star cognac of the 1840s blended for mixing. Bottled at 45 per cent, it is the cognac made for the bar's own classics, the Sidecar, the julep and Jerry Thomas's punches.
picks.note: The label now reads Ferrand, not Pierre Ferrand; the Library entry is under Pierre Ferrand; confirm the current label. It was made with the house's owner, its cellar master and a cocktail historian, all living: describe them by role only. Production facts here rest on retailers and reviews; confirm on the house's own page.

alternates.why: A Jarnac house that bottles only Grande Champagne and starts its range at XO; Pale & Dry is its long aged, uncoloured style.
A Jarnac house whose Rare is a Fine Champagne blend of Grande and Petite Champagne at 40 per cent; some markets label it Hine Rare Fine Champagne.

picks.why: A family estate at Eauze in the Bas-Armagnac, owned by the Grassa family since 1912, that makes its armagnac only from its own vines. The VSOP is the estate armagnac a bar can carry and the plain lesson that armagnac is a grower's spirit.
picks.note: Confirm the label wording and the stated age: one retailer gives at least seven years but mixes the VS Classique and VSOP sheets. The Library's process text (single column alambic, low strength) should be checked against the estate's own page before reuse.

picks.why: A house founded at Condom in 1851 by Pierre Etienne Janneau its spirit still aged in the cellars built that year. The VSOP is the house's blend at 40 per cent and a common first armagnac on a back bar, and the Atlas chapter already names the house.
picks.note: Sources call it one of the oldest houses, not the oldest; keep it that way. The VSOP's stated age differs (seven years from one retailer, the legal minimum elsewhere); confirm on the house's sheet. Janneau uses both the column still and the pot still; confirm which spirit goes into the VSOP before saying so.

picks.why: A single block estate at Sorbets in the Bas-Armagnac, founded in 1870 and run by the Lesgourgues family since 1974, that distils all four of its grapes, Baco, Colombard, Folle Blanche and Ugni Blanc. The VSOP shows what a whole estate's grapes give in one blend.
picks.note: Founding is 1870 in most sources and 1855 in one; the estate's size differs between listings. The family's present generation is living: keep names out.

picks.why: One of the two names under which the Delord family distillery at Lannepax has sold its armagnac since 1925, taken from Marie Duffau, who founded the firm with her husband Prosper Delord and their son. The Napoléon, at least six years old and 40 per cent, is the Bas-Armagnac a guest often meets first in a shop.
picks.note: The pick is the label; Delord makes it, so Delord is an alternate only and must not also stand as a pick. Confirm the founders' names and 1925 on the house's own page; sources are mostly retailers.

picks.why: An armagnac house that selects and ages casks from many Bas-Armagnac growers. Les Grands Assemblages are its blends by age, set against its single estate and single vintage Collection Unique, so the 20 Ans teaches how an armagnac eleveur works.
picks.note: The house's present head is living: describe him by role. Strength differs (43 or 40 per cent); confirm. Roquefort as the house's seat is from memory, not from these searches; confirm or leave out.

alternates.why: The family distillery at Lannepax that also makes Marie Duffau; its 25 year old blends Baco, Folle Blanche, Ugni Blanc and Colombard. Use only if Marie Duffau is dropped.
An armagnac made at Panjas, mainly from Ugni Blanc, at 40 per cent, widely stocked in France and Britain.

picks.why: A family house of the Pays d'Auge, begun when Christian Drouin the elder bought a cider orchard farm near Honfleur in 1960, that double distils in pot stills and ages in a range of casks. Its young Sélection is the calvados a bar uses for the Widow's Kiss and the Corpse Reviver No. 1.
picks.note: Confirm the label wording of the young bottling (Sélection, and whether it reads Calvados Pays d'Auge) and its stated age. The family's present generations are living: keep names out. Sources differ on whether the distillery dates from 1960 or 1980.

picks.why: A Pont-l'Évêque house founded in 1821 and named for an innkeeper of the Pays d'Auge. Its VSOP is a Calvados Pays d'Auge of at least four years, double distilled, at 40 per cent, and a calvados a guest will often have seen in a shop.
picks.note: Ownership history is unclear (a 1998 sale by a related Pont-l'Évêque firm); leave owners out. Confirm that the VSOP label carries the Pays d'Auge appellation in the owner's market.

picks.why: A family house at Coquainvilliers founded in 1825 by Pierre-Auguste Boulard and still in his family. Its VSOP blends Pays d'Auge calvados of four to ten years, double distilled in pot stills, and shows the appellation's rounder apple fruit.
picks.note: The present head of the family is living: keep the name out. The house's claim to a hand in founding the Pays d'Auge appellation in 1942 is its own and should not stand in the why.

picks.why: The calvados of Maison Ferrand, the Cognac house, bottled at 40 per cent and aged about five years. It is a Pays d'Auge made with the shaker in mind, from a Cognac house that builds bottlings for bartenders.
picks.note: Where Daron is distilled is not stated in any source found; do not say. One retailer claims a Charentais pot still and orchards north of the Pays d'Auge; both unconfirmed. Maison Ferrand also owns the Ferrand cognac pick; the labels are separate.

picks.why: A family estate at the Clos de la Hurvanière, Saint-Cyr-du-Ronceray, in the Pays d'Auge, held by the Groults since the eighteenth century, that double distils over a wood fire. The Réserve 3 Ans is the estate's young calvados and a clear lesson in how fresh apple reads after three years.
picks.note: The young bottling was relaunched as 3 Ans in a new livery; confirm the exact label. All five picks are Pays d'Auge; plain AOC Calvados and the pear led Domfrontais have no pick, which the author may wish to say on the page.

alternates.why: A family estate at Cambremer in the Pays d'Auge, making calvados since 1865.
A house at Notre-Dame-de-Courson in the Pays d'Auge that starts its spirit in small new casks before older wood.

picks.why: The pisco of Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, a distillery whose origins are dated to 1684. Its Mosto Verde is an acholado, a blend of Quebranta, Torontel and Albilla, distilled from must whose fermentation is stopped early, and it teaches Peru's rule that pisco goes into the bottle at the strength it came off the still.
picks.note: The brand is being renamed Caravedo in some markets (Caravedo Mosto Verde, formerly Pisco Portón); confirm which name the owner's market prints and use that. Its master distiller is living: role only. Confirm 43 per cent.

picks.why: A Peruvian pisco distilled in pot stills at Bodega San Isidro in Ica, a bodega brought back into production in 2002 after decades shut. Primero Quebranta is pure Quebranta, the non aromatic grape that gives pisco its body, bottled at 41.3 per cent with no water added.
picks.note: The bodega's own founding date differs between sources (the 1800s, or about a century ago); leave it out.

picks.why: A Peruvian pisco founded in 2006, made from Quebranta in copper pot stills in the Ica Valley. The plain Macchu Pisco is the Quebranta pisco many American bars carry for the Pisco Sour, and its acholado and mosto verde siblings, La Diablada and Ñusta, show the other two styles.
picks.note: Founded by two sisters, both living; their surname differs between sources; keep them out of prose entirely. One retailer says it is made at the Tacama estate; confirm before naming a distillery. Strength is listed from 40 to 44 per cent; confirm the label.

picks.why: The pisco of a growers' cooperative of the Elqui Valley, formed at Vicuña in 1938 by 25 members when exports collapsed and now well over a thousand strong. It is the name that stands for Chilean pisco, made from muscat grapes under Chile's own appellation, and the Reservado is the bottling a Chilean bar pours for a Piscola.
picks.note: Whether Reservado is rested in wood differs between sources; confirm, and confirm the strength. The cooperative's founding is 1938 on its own site; 1931 and 1934 appear elsewhere. Chilean and Peruvian pisco law differ: the page must not carry Peru's rules over to Capel.

picks.why: The Chilean pisco of Miguel Torres, the Spanish wine family's Chilean house, first made about 2012 from Moscatel grapes of the Limarí Valley and distilled in copper in single batches. At 40 per cent it is the pisco on the owner's shelf and a clear lesson in an aromatic, muscat led Chilean pisco.
picks.note: The launch year rests on the house's own page (eighty four years after 1928) and a 2014 review; confirm. The member of the Torres family who created it is living: role only. Named for a former governor of Ovalle; confirm before telling the story.

alternates.why: A Peruvian pisco of Bodega San Nicolás in Pisco, named for the year of the first written record of pisco distilling, at 42 per cent.
A Chilean pisco of the Elqui Valley named for the poet Gabriela Mistral; the Especial 35 is barrel rested, from Pedro Ximénez and muscat.

picks.why: The brandy Pedro Domecq Loustau first sold under the name in 1874, held to be the first Brandy de Jerez and the one that brought sherry's solera to brandy. The Solera Reserva is the young, sherry cask brandy a guest names when he asks for Spanish brandy.
picks.note: The current label may read Fundador Sherry Cask Solera Reserva; confirm the form. Ownership is unclear in the sources (a González Byass page and Emperador's purchase in 2016); name the bodega only.

picks.why: The Solera Gran Reserva of Sánchez Romate in Jerez, aged through a solera of sherry casks to an average of about fifteen years. It is the old Brandy de Jerez a bar keeps for the guest who wants a Spanish brandy after dinner.
picks.note: The fifteen year average rests on one retailer; the council's own floor for Solera Gran Reserva is an average of ten years. Confirm on the bodega's sheet before stating an age.

picks.why: González Byass's brandy, distilled in two Charentais pot stills at its Los Arcos cellar in Jerez, which makes it one of the few Brandies de Jerez distilled as well as aged in the town. The Solera Gran Reserva averages about twelve years.
picks.note: The producer's notes call it the only brandy distilled in Jerez; another source says one of the few. Use 'one of the few' unless the bodega's own page is confirmed current.

picks.why: Osborne's Solera Gran Reserva, aged in Jerez through sherry casks, with vanilla and cocoa from the wood. It is a Brandy de Jerez a guest from Spain will often ask for by name.
picks.note: Confirm the bottling's average age and strength; neither was in the sources found. The Imperial XO is a separate, older bottling. Osborne's founding date was not searched; leave it out or confirm.

picks.flagship: Gran Duque d'Alba Solera Gran Reserva
picks.why: A Brandy de Jerez first made in 1945 by Williams & Humbert and named for the sixteenth century Duke of Alba. Distilled in pot stills from Palomino and Airén and aged about twelve years in oloroso casks, it is an old solera brandy an American bar can readily stock.
picks.note: Sources give its average age as twelve or ten years; confirm. Confirm it has a current American importer or cut that clause. Ownership of the bodega is disputed between sources; name Williams & Humbert only. This group is thinner at an American bar than cognac: Fundador and Cardenal Mendoza are met often, the other three mostly where a bar has a Spanish list.

alternates.why: A young Brandy de Jerez long sold across Spain; its current maker and bottling were not confirmed in this run and must be checked before use.
Osborne's young Brandy de Jerez, a separate label from Carlos I; its current bottling was not confirmed in this run and must be checked before use.

picks.flagship: Laird's Straight Apple Brandy Bottled in Bond
picks.why: The apple brandy of Laird & Company of Scobeyville, New Jersey, the name that stands for applejack. The bonded straight apple brandy, 100 per cent apple, at least four years in charred oak and 100 proof, is the bottle for a Jack Rose.
picks.note: Laird's own site gives four years; Difford's says three; use four. The firm calls itself the oldest family owned licensed distillery in America: a claim to keep out of the why. The family's founding date of 1780 was not confirmed in this run; confirm or leave out. The apple brandy is distilled in Virginia, from memory and not searched; confirm before saying where. Laird's Applejack, a blend with neutral spirit, and Straight Applejack 86 are separate bottlings: the page should say which is the lesson for 'applejack'.

picks.why: The California brandy of E. & J. Gallo, sold in VS, VSOP and XO and in flavours. It is an American brandy a guest is likely to name, and the VSOP, with vanilla, apple and oak, is the bottling to know.
picks.note: Many bars pour the E&J VS as the well brandy; the author may prefer VS as the flagship. Sales figures in trade sources are from mixed years; keep any ranking out of the page. The founders are dead; their company's present family owners are not to be named.

picks.why: A California brandy distilled in California and aged in Kentucky, which makes it the plain example of how much American brandy is grape spirit from the West aged in bourbon country.
picks.note: That Heaven Hill makes it and ages it at its Louisville plant rests on a 2011 blog and a retailer; confirm on Heaven Hill's own page before stating madeBy. The order's history with the brand is from memory; confirm or cut. Confirm the label's form ('The Christian Brothers' or 'Christian Brothers').

picks.why: The brandy of Korbel, the Russian River sparkling wine house, distilled from California grapes such as Colombard and Chenin Blanc and aged in used American oak. It is a plain, widely stocked California brandy for the shaker and the stirred brandy drink.
picks.note: That the Wisconsin Brandy Old Fashioned is built on Korbel is from memory, not searched; confirm before adding it to the why. Sources differ on the still (column, or pot for the older bottling) and on the age; confirm before stating either. Barrels from Brown-Forman's cooperage rest on a 2011 blog.

picks.why: A brandy distillery opened in the Butchertown district of Louisville in 2014, distilling California muscat and chenin blanc wine in large copper pot stills and ageing in used bourbon barrels. The American Craft Brandy, at 90 proof with no colour added, is the pot still American brandy a bartender should know beside the big California houses.
picks.note: Its founders are living: role only. Sources are 2015 to 2019; confirm the distillery is still working and who owns it today, and if it has closed, tell it in the past tense or swap in an alternate.

alternates.why: A California brandy counted among the four that make most American brandy sales; the flagship's name is from memory and must be confirmed.
A Mendocino County pot still brandy house; its current status and bottling were not searched in this run and must be confirmed before use.

left.why: Five labels a guest asks for by name do not exist: Laird's is the applejack a bar carries and the others are small local apple brandies. Applejack is taught through Laird's inside American brandy.

No brandy style exists in tools/caskstyles/plan.json, so every group here has style "": cognac, armagnac and calvados hang on their Cask Atlas chapters, and pisco, Brandy de Jerez and American brandy have neither a chapter nor a style yet.
